walkthroughs.body_html:
Solar Astronomy — a core area of A-Level Astronomy.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Solar Astronomy brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Solar Astronomy.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Length of the solar cycle (sunspot count)?
options: 1 year
11 years
22 years
50 years

mcqs.q: Charged particles streaming from the Sun are called?
options: Solar flares
Solar wind
Aurora
Cosmic rays

mcqs.q: Why is Jupiter classified as a gas giant?
options: Light from the most distant galaxies.
Its bulk is mostly hydrogen and helium with no defined solid surface.
It is made of fire.
It is mostly air like Earth's atmosphere.

mcqs.q: What is the cosmic microwave background?
options: It is made of fire.
Light from the most distant galaxies.
Relic radiation from when the universe became transparent, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
Background noise from human microwave ovens.

mcqs.q: Why don't we have a solar eclipse every new moon?
options: Because clouds block them.
It is made of fire.
The Moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the Sun's apparent position.
Eclipses happen randomly.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Coronal mass ejection”?
options: Huge eruption of plasma and magnetic field into space; can cause geomagnetic storms.
Cooler regions (~3,800 K) on the photosphere with strong magnetic fields (~0.3 T).
~11-year cycle of sunspot number and magnetic activity; full magnetic cycle is 22 years.
Continuous stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun's corona at 400-800 km/s.
